transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-26
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Maya Torres (Stormbreak Head of ML), Benji Park (Stormbreak Infra Lead), Claire O'Neil (Stormbreak CPO)

Summary: Short intake to understand Stormbreak's per-token budget, latency SLOs for interactive assistant, and whether Hosted/Dedicated/Private fits. Focus on batching, KV/prefix caching, and pilot scope for unit economics benchmarking.

Topics: pricing per-token assumptions; typical cache hit rates and impact on unit cost; Dedicated reserved capacity and burst; private deployment constraints (VPC, KMS); pilot scope and success criteria.

Action items (auto): see metadata list above.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Very excited to chat through Stormbreak's plans. I think we have about 50 minutes, is that right?
[00:15] Maya Torres: Yeah, that works. Thanks Alex. Quick context — we are building an internal assistant for customer support triage that will also be embedded into product flows. We have a hard monthly cap for inference spend of roughly $20k to $25k to start. Latency target for UI is around 150 to 200 ms average token latency, and p95 under 400 if possible.
[00:34] Alex Kim: Great — that's helpful. Quick intro from Priya who will head the technical piece.
[00:40] Priya Shah: Hi all — I focus on throughput and cache strategies. We'll want to map your QPS and prompt shapes to model variants and batching windows.
[00:48] Benji Park: Thanks. We currently run everything in GCP with some on-prem Kubernetes for sensitive customers. We prefer VPC options if possible. Also, our infra team is cautious about moving large volumes of PII off-prem.
[01:20] Alex Kim: Understood. One quick framing: when we talk about unit economics we usually separate three levers — model selection (and quantization), batching and concurrency policy, and caching/prefix hits. Each can move your per-token bill by orders of magnitude depending on hit rates and sequence lengths.
[01:55] Maya Torres: Can you give a concrete example?
[02:05] Priya Shah: Sure — rough ballpark: a 7B open checkpoint on Hosted with standard FP16 might have base token cost X, but with 4-bit quantization + optimized kernels that Redwood picks, you could see 2-3x lower compute cost per token. Then if your sessions reuse recent context (prefix caching/KV cache), effective tokens billed drop because we serve much from cache or avoid re-encoding the prefix.
[02:40] Maya Torres: When you say 'tokens billed' — is that our bill or the raw tokens processed? We want to understand the difference.
[02:50] Alex Kim: Good question. Hosted billing is on tokens generated plus input tokens in most models; but Redwood's pricing examples in a pilot show "effective tokens" after cache hits. So if you have a 60% prefix cache hit, the effective billable tokens can be 40% of raw. We'll share a worked example.
[03:10] Benji Park: Is that cache at the request-routing layer or inside the GPU runtime?
[03:20] Priya Shah: Both. We do prefix and KV caching inside the runtime — that avoids recompute on the GPU. There's also request-level caches at the router for deterministic replies. For things like chat where recent context is reused, runtime KV cache is the big win.
[03:45] Claire O'Neil: Our procurement team will ask about committed spend for Dedicated; what's typical lock-in and flex?
[03:55] Alex Kim: Dedicated is reserved GPU pools — typically monthly or annual commits. You get predictable throughput and lower unit cost per token, and priority routing. We also support mixed modes: a base reserved seat plus burst into Hosted. For procurement, we can lay out contract terms; commitment levels map to different discounts.
[04:25] Maya Torres: For our $20k/month budget, are we likely Hosted or Dedicated?
[04:32] Priya Shah: It depends on usage shape. If you have steady QPS and heavy sync traffic with long contexts, Dedicated tends to be better. If it's spiky and low average usage, Hosted is easier to start with. Also, pilot data will tell us — we'll run benchmarks to estimate per-100k token costs under your workload.
[04:55] Benji Park: We expect bursty traffic during product launches — a 5-10x spike for an hour. Can Redwood do burst capacity if we're Dedicated?
[05:07] Alex Kim: Yes — Dedicated has configurable burst options; you can pay for baseline reserved capacity and allow controlled burst into Hosted or extra dedicated nodes. We'll show pricing tradeoffs.
[05:20] Maya Torres: We care about latency — you mentioned batching windows. How does batching affect tail latency for interactive chat?
[05:29] Priya Shah: Batching increases throughput but can increase latency due to wait windows. Redwood's runtime supports adaptive batching with latency SLOs — so you can set a per-route latency target and the runtime trades off batch size. For your UI targets (150–200 ms average), we'd tune batch flush thresholds and use prefix cache to reduce tokens.
[05:55] Alex Kim: Also, model selection matters — smaller models or trimmed context can get you under 200ms more reliably. There's sometimes an accuracy tradeoff we should validate in evals.
[06:10] Benji Park: How accurate are your cost models? We want to avoid surprises.
[06:18] Priya Shah: We'll provide a pilot benchmark harness that we run on your prompt set. It uses your real prompts and QPS to produce a report: latency distribution, tokens generated, cache hit rate, and projected monthly spend under several hosting mixes. Past pilots have been within ~10–15% of realized costs after tuning.
[06:42] Maya Torres: That's helpful. On security, Claire, anything specific?
[06:48] Claire O'Neil: Yes — we need SOC2 plus KMS-based key management for model inputs and logs. For private hosting we might want an on-prem installer for air-gapped customers.
[07:05] Alex Kim: Redwood Private supports customer-managed VPC and KMS integrations; we also offer an on-prem package for fully air-gapped. There are extra ops and licensing costs for Private, which we will enumerate.
[07:30] Benji Park: If we go Private — do we still get Redwood's console and telemetry?
[07:36] Priya Shah: You get a private control plane option: the console and observability are available via a secure connection. For fully air-gapped there are more manual workflows.
[07:50] Maya Torres: Let's dig into the pilot. What would a 2-week pilot look like to validate unit economics?
[07:58] Alex Kim: Typical pilot: week 1 — ingest representative prompt set, run baseline tests on Hosted and a Dedicated baseline, measure cache behaviors and latency. Week 2 — iterate on batching/flush thresholds, test quantized model variants, and simulate bursts. We'll share a workbook with per-token projections. Priya will own the harness.
[08:20] Priya Shah: We'll ask you to provide: canonical prompt set, expected QPS distribution (minute-level or hourly), and a target SLO definition. We'll run automated runs and return a CSV with token counts, cache rates, median/p95 latencies, and cost projection scenarios.
[08:38] Benji Park: On the model side, are we locked into a single model? We might want fallback smaller models if latency spikes.
[08:45] Alex Kim: Redwood supports routing policies and automatic fallback to compatible variants — you can route by latency/cost and do canary rollouts. So a hot path can use a low-latency model while deeper completions use a larger one.
[09:00] Maya Torres: Let's talk numbers — can you walk through a worked example? For simplicity: 100k generated tokens/day, avg sequence length 120 tokens, 60% prefix reuse.
[09:12] Priya Shah: Quick math rough: raw tokens/day = 12M. With 60% prefix cache effective tokens might be ~4.8M. If Hosted per-1M tokens is $X (we will provide actual numbers) — multiply accordingly. With Dedicated reserved discount, that per-1M goes down. Also quantized kernel lowers compute portion further. The pilot will convert these placeholders into firm $ figures.
[09:46] Claire O'Neil: Are the prefixes typically small? Our conversation histories can be several KB long for context.
[09:53] Priya Shah: Runtime KV cache stores per-session past key/value pairs so you do avoid re-encoding long prefixes; hit rates depend on session reuse and how much context changes. For long tail contexts you get diminishing returns.
[10:10] Benji Park: Does cache require sticky sessions to a specific GPU/server?
[10:16] Priya Shah: There is sticky routing for warm KV cache, but Redwood also supports transparent cache migration and cold-warm fallbacks. We'll detail the tradeoffs — sticky gives best latency but has lower global utilization.
[10:36] Alex Kim: One thing customers often miss — you should instrument early for effective tokens and separate input vs output tokens in your billing projection spreadsheet.
[10:48] Maya Torres: Makes sense. Can we get a sample spreadsheet?
[10:52] Alex Kim: Yes, I'll send one after the call — tailored to your 100k/day example.
[11:00] Priya Shah: Quick aside: quantization path — not all models compress equally. We'll recommend specific model checkpoints with Redwood-verified performance.
[11:12] Maya Torres: What's the expected impact of quantization on answer quality?
[11:17] Priya Shah: Usually small regressions for many tasks; we'll run evals on your prompt set to validate. If it's an unacceptable drop, we recommend caching and routing instead of aggressive quantization.
[11:30] Benji Park: On billing granularity — do you bill at the token or request/second granularity for Hosted?
[11:36] Alex Kim: Hosted is token-based. Dedicated includes a capacity commitment and then metered over usage; pricing components include reserved capacity + overage rules.
[11:48] Maya Torres: Procurement will want a worst-case monthly spend number if we do burst to Hosted.
[11:54] Alex Kim: We'll model worst-case and most-likely scenarios in the workbook — show 95th percentile monthly spend and a capped burst plan.
[12:30] [long pause while screenshare note] Priya Shah: (screenshare) here's a sample run from a previous pilot — you can see cache hit curve over time and how latency improves as cache warms. Note: transcription error — model name shows as 'Rwood-7B' in slide.
[13:05] Maya Torres: The warmup time concerns me; for product launches we need fast ramp.
[13:12] Priya Shah: For launches we recommend pre-warming using synthetic traffic and short TTLs for prefixes, plus a burst plan. Also pre-warming KV cache per user cohort helps.
[13:35] Benji Park: Does Redwood provide scripts for synthetic warmup?
[13:39] Priya Shah: Yes — included in the pilot harness. We'll share a runner that replays traffic at desired rates.
[14:05] Alex Kim: Let's talk procurement timeline — Claire, do you have target decision date?
[14:10] Claire O'Neil: We're aiming to pick a vendor and sign pilot terms by mid-May (around 2026-05-15) so we can run a pilot before a June launch.
[14:22] Alex Kim: That's doable. We'll prioritize the pricing workbook and security docs to meet that date.
[14:32] Maya Torres: On data retention and logs — we need 30-day retention for usage logs and ability to purge.
[14:38] Priya Shah: Redwood supports configurable retention and per-tenant logging controls; for Private/on-prem you control logs entirely.
[15:05] Benji Park: One more technical: do you support hardware-specific optimizations? We use A100s internally.
[15:12] Priya Shah: Yes — Redwood runtime chooses kernels per hardware and we publish performance profiles per GPU class, including A100 and forthcoming L4/TSM variants. We'll align on the GPU profile for Dedicated.
[15:34] Maya Torres: If we do a hybrid — reserved Dedicated for baseline and Hosted for burst — what's the expected blended per-token cost change?
[15:42] Alex Kim: Blending increases predictability while still enabling capacity; the blended cost is weighted average of reserved discounted rate and Hosted on-demand. We'll model scenarios: 70/30 reserved vs burst, 90/10, etc.
[16:05] Claire O'Neil: Any legal gotchas we should expect for Private deployments?
[16:12] Alex Kim: Mostly standard stuff: data transfer terms, liability, and support SLAs. For on-prem air-gapped we add professional services to install and run health checks.
[16:30] Maya Torres: Ok — next steps recap?
[16:35] Alex Kim: I'll share pricing workbook and example pilot report by 2026-04-29.
[16:39] Priya Shah: I'll schedule the 2-hour kickoff pilot planning meeting and attach the harness doc.
[16:44] Maya Torres: We'll circulate the prompt set and QPS profile by 2026-05-03.
[16:50] Claire O'Neil: Procurement will follow up with an initial SOW request and compliance checklist.

[25:00] [longer discussion on specific cache TTLs and session stickiness — technical details omitted for brevity in this transcript export but captured in the pilot doc link]

[33:00] Benji Park: Circling back to the math — we'll need a conservative worst-case cost for CFO review.
[33:08] Alex Kim: We'll include a 'worst-case spike' tab in the workbook assuming no cache hits and high sequence lengths; that gives you an upper bound.
[40:00] Maya Torres: One final question — do you have references of customers in fintech/retail who did similar pilot sizing?
[40:08] Alex Kim: Yes, we'll share a short anonymized case study.
[47:00] Claire O'Neil: If we move forward on pilot, what are the billing terms?
[47:07] Alex Kim: Pilots are typically product/credit-backed with usage caps; if you proceed to Dedicated we'd convert commitments into a month-to-month billing arrangement or annual contract per your preference.
[47:40] Maya Torres: Ok that covers our main concerns. Thanks a lot.
[47:45] Alex Kim: Great — appreciate the time. We'll follow up with the docs and calendar invites.
[51:30] Priya Shah: Quick note — transcription may mis-spell some product names in the shared slides; we'll attach original files.
[51:50] Alex Kim: Thanks everyone.
[51:55] Maya Torres: Bye.

Recap (auto): Pilot scope: ingest prompts, run Hosted vs Dedicated baseline, tune batching and caching, report token economics. Success criteria: show a path to meet 150–200 ms median latency within $20–25k monthly budget, or present tradeoffs if not feasible.

References/Links mentioned: pilot-harness-doc (shared post-call), sample-pricing-workbook (to be shared), security-brief (SOC2/KMS notes).
